set1.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
set1.q: Which features characterize acute hypotension?
opts: Waxing, waning, intermittent symptoms
Waxing and waning with intermittent symptoms describes chronic hypotension, where the underlying cause may be unavoidable.
Gradual onset with no symptoms ever
Acute hypotension is usually symptomatic and sudden. A slow, silent course does not fit its description.
Persistent lows from an unavoidable cause
An underlying cause that may be unavoidable is a feature of chronic hypotension, such as reduced ejection fraction heart failure.
Sudden onset, symptoms, a specific trigger
Correct. Acute hypotension is of sudden onset, usually symptomatic and usually with specific triggers, unlike chronic hypotension, which waxes and wanes.

set1.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
set1.q: Which cause of hypotension is typically acute?
opts: Cardiomyopathy
Cardiomyopathy is a cardiogenic cause of chronic hypotension, which waxes and wanes and may have an unavoidable cause.
Heart failure
Reduced ejection fraction heart failure is grouped with cardiomyopathy as a cardiogenic cause of chronic hypotension.
Ventricular pump weakness
A weak pump from cardiomyopathy or heart failure causes chronic rather than acute hypotension.
Toxic exposure
Correct. Toxic exposure and medication-mediated overdose produce acute hypotension of sudden onset with a specific trigger.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: How is postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome defined in adults?
opts: Heart rate up over 10 when lying down
Symptoms of the syndrome usually improve when lying down; the criteria are about the rise within 10 minutes of standing.
Heart rate up over 30, or above 120, in 10 minutes
Correct. The heart rate rises by more than 30 beats per minute, or exceeds 120, within 10 minutes of standing, and usually improves when lying down.
Systolic fall over 20 mmHg in 3 minutes
A systolic fall of more than 20 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing is the orthostatic hypotension criterion, a pressure rather than a heart rate test.
Heart rate up over 30, or above 120, in 3 minutes
The window for this syndrome is 10 minutes of standing. Three minutes is the window for the orthostatic pressure criteria.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for hypotension in the lecture topic list for the following populations. a. infant b. child c. adolescent d. adult e. elderly
set1.q: In whom is vasovagal syncope most commonly seen?
opts: Adults with diabetes
Long-standing diabetes is a cause of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension through autonomic neuropathy, not a feature of vasovagal syncope.
Young women
Correct. Vasovagal syncope, the common faint, is most commonly seen in young women, and its triggers include fear, pain, heat and prolonged standing.
Older men
Older men feature in situational micturition syncope and in cardiogenic syncope, but vasovagal syncope is most common in young women.
Adolescent boys
Adolescence matters for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome thresholds, and that syndrome, too, affects women more than men.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: Which type of reflex syncope is known as the common faint?
opts: Situational syncope
Situational syncope is the reflex type triggered by bodily functions or physical actions, such as micturition syncope.
Neurogenic syncope
Neurogenic syncope is an orthostatic type caused by autonomic dysfunction, such as from diabetes or Parkinson disease.
Cardiogenic syncope
Cardiogenic syncope comes from an arrhythmia, structural disease or a vascular cause, not from a reflex.
Vasovagal syncope
Correct. Vasovagal syncope is the most common type, known as the common faint, and is most commonly seen in young women.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: What should a patient with recurrent reflex syncope be asked to keep?
opts: A weekly weight chart
Weight charts suit volume questions. Reflex syncope is tracked with a log of when and how often episodes occur.
A home blood pressure average
An averaged home pressure hides the transient reflex episodes. The log records the pattern and frequency of the faints themselves.
A log of pattern and frequency
Correct. A patient log helps determine the pattern and frequency of episodes, which supports a diagnosis built mainly on the history.
A daily blood glucose diary
Glucose checks exclude hypoglycemia, a non-hypotensive cause, but the recommended record for reflex syncope is an episode log.

set1.io: Define hypotension
set1.q: Why should a single low reading be interpreted cautiously?
opts: Pressure never varies within a day
Pressure does vary, which is exactly why a single measurement is only a snapshot and needs context.
Each reading is a snapshot in time
Correct. A reading is a snapshot in time, and it must also be weighed against age, comorbidities and the possibility of relative hypotension.
Cuffs overestimate low pressures
Device error is not the concern raised. The caution is that one reading captures a single moment in a pressure that varies.
Low readings are always artifact
Low readings can be real and clinically important. They are interpreted in context rather than dismissed as artifact.

set1.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set1.q: Which history favors reflex syncope over a seizure?
opts: Brief prodrome, then rapid recovery
Correct. A brief prodrome of warmth, nausea, sweating and lightheadedness followed by rapid recovery favors reflex syncope over seizure or a primary arrhythmia.
Tongue biting and long confusion
Tongue biting and prolonged confusion afterward point toward seizure; their absence is what supports syncope.
Rhythmic jerking and incontinence
Convulsive movements and incontinence unrelated to urination point toward seizure rather than a reflex faint.
No warning, then palpitations
Abrupt collapse without warning after palpitations points toward cardiogenic syncope from an arrhythmia.

set1.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
set1.q: Which cause of hypotension is classed as chronic?
opts: Bacteremia
Infection, from bacteremia through sepsis to septic shock, causes long-lasting acute hypotension rather than chronic hypotension.
Cardiomyopathy
Correct. Cardiogenic causes, reduced ejection fraction heart failure and cardiomyopathy, produce chronic hypotension, whose cause may be unavoidable.
Medication overdose
Medication-mediated overdose is a toxic cause producing acute hypotension, with sudden onset and a specific trigger.
Toxic exposure
Toxic exposure causes acute hypotension. Chronic hypotension comes from cardiogenic causes such as cardiomyopathy.

set1.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set1.q: How should a suspected vascular cause of syncope be evaluated?
opts: Electively, with an outpatient monitor
Outpatient monitoring suits a suspected arrhythmia. Vascular causes such as dissection or embolism need emergent evaluation.
Routinely, with a symptom log
An episode log supports reflex syncope. A suspected vascular catastrophe cannot wait for a pattern to emerge.
Later, with a tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing belongs to postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and has no role in excluding a vascular emergency.
Emergently, in the emergency department
Correct. Vascular causes, dissection, aneurysm, stroke and pulmonary embolism, need emergent testing in the emergency department plus cardiology consultation.

set1.io: Define hypotension
set1.q: Why is hypotension not the final diagnosis in a patient who faints?
opts: It is defined only by the symptoms
Hypotension is a measured fall in pressure below normal, an objective sign, and it still points to a cause that must be identified.
It results from an underlying cause
Correct. Syncope is the result of symptomatic hypotension, and treatment is aimed at the underlying cause, the real diagnosis, such as volume loss, a medication, a reflex or a cardiac problem.
It is too rare a finding to name
Low blood pressure is common rather than rare. It is left off as a final diagnosis because it is the consequence of another process that needs naming.
It always resolves before assessment
It often persists, as in chronic hypotension, which waxes and wanes. Resolution is not the reason; the need to find its underlying cause is.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: In a patient with a normal baseline pressure, which systolic change on standing meets the orthostatic criterion?
opts: A fall of more than 20 mmHg within 10 minutes
The orthostatic window is 3 minutes of standing. Ten minutes is the window for the heart rate criteria of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome.
A heart rate rise of more than 30 per minute
A heart rate rise of more than 30 per minute on standing belongs to postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, not the pressure-based orthostatic criteria.
A fall of more than 20 mmHg within 3 minutes
Correct. A systolic fall of more than 20 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing meets the criterion; a diastolic fall of more than 10 mmHg within 3 minutes is the companion criterion.
A fall of more than 10 mmHg within 3 minutes
More than 10 mmHg within 3 minutes is the diastolic criterion. The systolic threshold with a normal baseline is more than 20 mmHg.

set1.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set1.q: Which of these is a symptom rather than a sign?
opts: A heart rate of 148
A heart rate is an objective measurement recorded by the examiner, which makes it a sign rather than something the patient reports.
Dry oral mucous membranes
Dry mucous membranes are observed on examination, making them an objective sign, here one suggesting volume depletion.
Lightheadedness
Correct. Lightheadedness is a subjective change that the patient feels and reports, whereas signs are objective and measurable, such as vital signs.
A standing pressure drop
A measured fall in pressure on standing is objective and measurable, which makes it a sign rather than a symptom.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for hypotension in the lecture topic list for the following populations. a. infant b. child c. adolescent d. adult e. elderly
set1.q: Who is typically affected by postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome?
opts: Infants, equally both sexes
The syndrome is described in people aged 15 to 50, usually women more than men, rather than in infants of either sex.
Over 60, with Parkinson disease
Parkinson disease in older adults causes neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, with a pressure fall and minimal heart rate rise.
Ages 15 to 50, more often women
Correct. The syndrome affects people aged 15 to 50, usually women more than men, and is associated with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Over 70, more often men
Older men are typical of situational micturition syncope. This syndrome affects a younger group, more often women.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for hypotension in the lecture topic list for the following populations. a. infant b. child c. adolescent d. adult e. elderly
set1.q: Which of these is a cause of non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?
opts: Advanced age
Correct. Advanced age is listed with hypovolemia and medication as a cause of non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension in the elderly.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is associated with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, which affects ages 15 to 50.
Emotional triggers
Emotional stress and fear are triggers of vasovagal syncope, which is most commonly seen in young women.
Autoimmune disorders
Autoimmune disorders are listed behind neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, the form with a minimal heart rate rise.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: Which systolic threshold applies when baseline pressure is elevated with supine hypertension (high pressure while lying flat)?
opts: A fall of more than 30 mmHg
Correct. With an elevated baseline or supine hypertension the systolic fall must exceed 30 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing to meet the orthostatic criterion.
A fall of more than 20 mmHg
More than 20 mmHg is the systolic threshold for a patient with a normal baseline. An elevated baseline raises the bar to more than 30 mmHg.
A fall of more than 10 mmHg
More than 10 mmHg is the diastolic criterion. The systolic threshold with supine hypertension is more than 30 mmHg.
A fall of more than 40 mmHg
Forty is the heart rate rise that defines the tachycardia syndrome in adolescents. The systolic threshold here is more than 30 mmHg.

set1.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set1.q: Which subtypes are recognized within reflex syncope?
opts: Vasodepressor, cardioinhibitory and mixed
Correct. The standard syncope classification splits reflex syncope by whether the vessels dilate, the heart slows, or both, all under an inappropriate reflex.
Neurogenic, non-neurogenic and mixed
Neurogenic and non-neurogenic are the two kinds of orthostatic syncope, separated by whether the autonomic nervous system itself has failed.
Arrhythmic, structural and vascular
These are the three types of cardiogenic syncope, each with its own work-up, rather than subtypes of the reflex group.
Primary, secondary and drug-induced
Primary, secondary and drug-induced autonomic failure belong to orthostatic hypotension in the classification, not to reflex syncope.

set1.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set1.q: What separates near-syncope from syncope?
opts: Recovery that needs medical treatment
Neither requires treatment to recover. Syncope ends in spontaneous recovery, and near-syncope never reaches loss of consciousness.
Warning symptoms without losing consciousness
Correct. Near-syncope, or presyncope, is the dizziness, lightheadedness and tunnel vision that precede a faint; syncope adds the transient loss of consciousness and postural tone.
A longer loss of consciousness than syncope
Near-syncope involves no loss of consciousness at all. It describes the symptoms experienced before a faint rather than a longer version of one.
A cardiac rather than a reflex cause
Both can arise from any cause of symptomatic hypotension. The difference is whether consciousness is lost, not which organ system is responsible.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: Which feature is often present in neurogenic but usually absent in non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?
opts: Volume depletion
Volume depletion runs the other way: often present in non-neurogenic and usually absent in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
A marked heart rate rise
A significant heart rate rise belongs to the non-neurogenic form, where the intact autonomic system compensates for the fall.
Recent diuretic use
Diuretics are an example cause of the non-neurogenic form, acting through volume loss rather than through autonomic damage.
Autonomic symptoms
Correct. Autonomic symptoms are often present with autonomic failure and usually absent when the cause is volume loss or medication.

set1.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set1.q: Which test evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope?
opts: Echocardiogram
Correct. Structural causes, infarction, cardiomyopathy, heart failure and valve disease, are evaluated with echocardiography or stress echocardiography plus cardiology consultation.
Tilt-table test
The tilt-table test diagnoses postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and has low sensitivity, so it is not the structural work-up.
Symptom log
An episode log supports the history-based diagnosis of reflex syncope, not the evaluation of structural heart disease.
Orthostatic vitals
Supine and standing vital signs diagnose orthostatic hypotension; structural heart disease needs imaging of the heart.

set1.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
set1.q: Where are vasopressors such as norepinephrine and vasopressin used for hypotension?
opts: Outpatient use for the tachycardia syndrome
The tachycardia syndrome is treated with water, salt and fludrocortisone, not with vasopressors.
Emergency department and intensive care only
Correct. Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, phenylephrine and vasopressin are listed for the emergency department and intensive care unit only.
Primary care for chronic hypotension
Chronic hypotension in primary care is managed by treating its cause and education; pressors are not outpatient drugs.
Home use for recurrent reflex syncope
Recurrent reflex syncope is treated with trigger avoidance and safety precautions rather than pressors at home.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: Which drug is best used with neurogenic syncope?
opts: Midodrine
Correct. Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope, but it is avoided with supine hypertension, severe heart disease and chronic kidney disease.
Fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone is best with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and is avoided in heart failure.
Droxidopa
Droxidopa has only mild efficacy and is usually added to midodrine or fludrocortisone rather than chosen first.
Vasopressin
Vasopressin is among the pressors reserved for the emergency department and intensive care, not outpatient neurogenic syncope.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: What defines non-neurogenic orthostatic syncope?
opts: A reflex faint after a bodily function
A faint triggered by a bodily function such as urination is situational reflex syncope, a transient reflex rather than a sustained postural drop.
A heart rate rise without a pressure drop
A marked heart rate rise on standing without a qualifying pressure fall describes postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, not orthostatic hypotension.
A postural drop without autonomic failure
Correct. It is a sustained fall in pressure on standing or sitting upright that is not a result of autonomic dysfunction, usually from hypovolemia, medication or advanced age.
A postural drop from autonomic nerve damage
Autonomic nerve damage defines the neurogenic form, where the heart rate rises only minimally as pressure falls on standing.

set1.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set1.q: Which three groups make up the most common causes of syncope?
opts: Neurogenic, septic and toxic
Neurogenic is only one branch of orthostatic syncope, and sepsis and toxic exposure are causes of hypotension listed separately from the three syncope groups.
Situational, vasovagal and seizure
Situational and vasovagal are both reflex syncope, and seizure is a non-hypotensive cause. The three main groups are orthostatic, reflex and cardiogenic.
Arrhythmic, structural and anxiety
Arrhythmic and structural are two of the three cardiogenic types, and anxiety is a non-hypotensive cause of syncope rather than a main group.
Orthostatic, reflex and cardiogenic
Correct. Orthostatic syncope divides into neurogenic and non-neurogenic, reflex syncope into situational and vasovagal, and cardiogenic syncope into arrhythmia, structural and vascular.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: Why is fludrocortisone avoided in heart failure?
opts: It worsens kidney function
Chronic kidney disease is a listed reason to avoid midodrine. Fludrocortisone is avoided in heart failure because of fluid retention.
It causes salt and water retention
Correct. Fludrocortisone causes salt and water retention, which helps the tachycardia syndrome but is why it is avoided in congestive heart failure.
It causes supine hypertension
Supine hypertension is the setting in which midodrine is avoided and droxidopa is preferred, not the stated fludrocortisone concern.
It slows the heart rate sharply
Heart rate slowing is not the listed problem. The concern in heart failure is the salt and water it retains.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: Which measures are first-line for orthostatic syncope?
opts: Vasopressors started in primary care
Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, phenylephrine and vasopressin are for the emergency department and intensive care only.
Fludrocortisone for every patient
Fludrocortisone is best suited to postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and is avoided in heart failure because it retains salt and water.
Strict fluid restriction every day
Restricting fluid worsens volume depletion, the usual cause of non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, rather than treating it.
Slow position changes, treat the cause
Correct. Slow positional changes limit the drop on standing, and treating the underlying cause addresses the real diagnosis behind the hypotension.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: Which conditions are examples of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension causes?
opts: Emotional stress and pain
These are triggers of vasovagal reflex syncope, a transient reflex event rather than a disease of the autonomic nervous system.
Arrhythmia and valve disease
These are cardiogenic causes of syncope, worked up with an electrocardiogram, monitoring and echocardiography rather than orthostatic vitals.
Diabetes and Parkinson disease
Correct. Both, like multiple system atrophy, damage the autonomic nervous system, which is why these patients show a pressure fall with only a minimal heart rate rise on standing.
Diarrhea and hemorrhage
These are the examples of non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, where volume loss or medication lowers pressure and the heart rate rises significantly.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: Inadequate venous return causing orthostatic hypotension has which two sources?
opts: Volume depletion and venous pooling
Correct. In the standard classification these lower cardiac output on standing, while structural or drug-induced autonomic failure lowers peripheral resistance instead.
Primary and secondary autonomic failure
Autonomic failure, primary or secondary, is the structural-damage branch of orthostatic hypotension, acting through low peripheral resistance.
Arrhythmia and structural heart disease
These are sources of cardiac syncope, where the heart itself fails to maintain output, rather than problems of venous return on standing.
Emotional stress and prolonged standing
These are triggers of vasovagal reflex syncope, which acts through an inappropriate reflex rather than through inadequate venous return.

set1.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set1.q: Which quick test excludes hypoglycemia as the cause of a faint?
opts: A blood glucose level
Correct. A normal blood glucose rules out hypoglycemia, one of the non-hypotensive causes of syncope, alongside blood counts and a metabolic panel for infection or metabolic causes.
A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and tells nothing about the blood sugar at the time of a faint.
An echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope, such as cardiomyopathy or valve disease, not hypoglycemia.
Orthostatic vital signs
Supine and standing vital signs diagnose orthostatic hypotension; a low sugar is excluded with a blood glucose measurement.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set1.q: When hypotension is caused by a medication, what is the first step?
opts: Start fludrocortisone therapy
Fludrocortisone is best with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and retains salt and water, so it does not fix a drug side effect.
Refer for a tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing belongs to the tachycardia syndrome. A medication cause is managed by reducing or removing the medication.
Reduce or remove the medication
Correct. The principle is to remove the offending agent or trigger: iatrogenic hypotension is treated by reducing or removing the responsible medication.
Add midodrine to counter it
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope. Adding a drug to offset another leaves the offending agent in place when it could be reduced.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: In vasovagal syncope, what finally causes the loss of consciousness?
opts: Cerebral flow below autoregulation
Correct. Bradycardia, vasodilation and reduced output drop systolic pressure until cerebral blood flow falls below the limits of autoregulation and consciousness is lost.
Seizure activity across the cortex
Seizure is a non-hypotensive cause of transient loss of consciousness; vasovagal syncope works through reduced cerebral blood flow.
Low blood glucose in the brain
Hypoglycemia is a separate, non-hypotensive cause of syncope that is excluded with a blood glucose measurement.
A ventricular rhythm stopping flow
A ventricular arrhythmia is a cardiogenic cause of syncope, recognized by abrupt collapse without warning and confirmed on an electrocardiogram.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: How is reflex syncope diagnosed?
opts: Mainly by serum electrolytes
Electrolytes help exclude a metabolic contributor, but reflex syncope is diagnosed from the history of its triggers.
Mainly by the history
Correct. History is the most important portion of diagnosing reflex syncope, summed up as history, history, history, with a log of pattern and frequency.
Mainly by tilt-table testing
The tilt-table test is listed for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, and a negative result tells little given its 40% sensitivity.
Mainly by echocardiography
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope, such as cardiomyopathy or valve disease, not reflex syncope.

set2.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set2.q: Which work-up is listed for arrhythmic cardiogenic syncope?
opts: Electrocardiogram, monitor, stress test
Correct. Arrhythmia is investigated with an electrocardiogram, cardiac monitoring and a stress test, together with cardiology consultation.
Echocardiogram and stress echocardiogram
Echocardiography and stress echocardiography are the work-up for structural causes such as cardiomyopathy and valve disease.
Emergent testing in the emergency room
Emergent testing in the emergency department is reserved for vascular causes such as dissection, stroke and pulmonary embolism.
Tilt-table test and an episode log
A tilt-table test belongs to the tachycardia syndrome and a log to reflex syncope; neither is the arrhythmia work-up.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: Why does pressure fall on standing in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?
opts: Too little norepinephrine from sympathetic nerves
Correct. Inadequate norepinephrine release from sympathetic postganglionic neurons means the vessels fail to constrict and the heart rate rises less than expected.
Excess vagal outflow triggered by fear
A surge of vagal outflow with sympathetic inhibition is the vasovagal reflex chain, which is transient and triggered rather than sustained.
Reduced circulating volume from fluid loss
Reduced volume is the non-neurogenic mechanism, and there the intact autonomic system drives a significant heart rate rise.
A fast ventricular rhythm reducing filling
A rapid rhythm lowering output is an arrhythmic cardiogenic cause, not a failure of the autonomic response to standing.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: Which are listed causes of non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?
opts: Hypovolemia, medication and advanced age
Correct. Dehydration, blood loss, poor intake and medication use lower output or impair vasoconstriction without any primary autonomic disorder.
Diabetic, genetic and autoimmune disorders
These are the disorders behind the neurogenic form, where autonomic damage prevents appropriate vasoconstriction and heart rate rise.
Fear, pain and prolonged standing
These trigger vasovagal reflex syncope, a transient vagal surge with sympathetic inhibition, not a sustained orthostatic drop.
Arrhythmia, infarction and embolism
These are cardiogenic causes of syncope across the arrhythmic, structural and vascular groups rather than orthostatic causes.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: Which examination finding supports diabetic autonomic neuropathy in a patient with orthostatic syncope?
opts: A heart rate above 120 standing
A heart rate exceeding 120 within 10 minutes of standing is a criterion for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, not an examination sign of neuropathy.
Reduced sensation in both feet
Correct. Decreased vibration and light-touch sensation in both feet marks long-standing diabetes with peripheral neuropathy, which supports diabetic autonomic neuropathy as the cause.
Dry oral mucous membranes
Dry mucous membranes point to volume depletion, the usual cause of non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
A rapid, regular rhythm
A rapid regular rhythm with hypotension raises concern for an arrhythmia and cardiogenic syncope rather than autonomic neuropathy.

set2.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set2.q: Which factors further predispose an older man to micturition syncope?
opts: Prior infarction, low ejection fraction
Prior infarction and reduced ejection fraction raise concern for cardiogenic syncope, such as nonsustained ventricular tachycardia.
Alcohol, dehydration, an alpha-1 blocker
Correct. Alcohol use, relative dehydration and an alpha-1 blocker taken with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor add to the risk of hypotension during nocturnal voiding.
Diabetes, Parkinson disease, neuropathy
These cause neurogenic orthostatic hypotension through autonomic failure, with a minimal heart rate rise on standing.
Fear, pain and heat exposure
Fear, pain and heat are triggers of vasovagal syncope rather than factors that predispose to micturition syncope.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: Which advice suits a patient with orthostatic syncope?
opts: Restrict fluids each morning
Restricting fluid worsens volume depletion, a common cause of non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
Avoid all physical activity
Activity itself is not the problem; the advice targets the moment of standing, with slow positional changes.
Change position slowly
Correct. Slow positional changes are listed treatment for orthostatic syncope, alongside treating the underlying cause, the real diagnosis.
Stand up quickly to adapt
Standing abruptly is the provoking event in orthostatic syncope; the advice is to change position slowly.

set2.io: Define hypotension
set2.q: What is the expected course of a syncopal episode?
opts: Brief and self-limited
Correct. Syncope is by definition transient and self-limited, followed by spontaneous recovery, which is part of what separates it from seizure.
Prolonged coma needing support
Prolonged unconsciousness needing support falls outside the definition of syncope, which is brief and self-limited.
Recovery only after glucose
Recovery after glucose describes hypoglycemia, a non-hypotensive cause, rather than the spontaneous recovery of syncope.
Recovery with lasting confusion
Prolonged confusion afterward points toward seizure; syncope ends in rapid, complete recovery.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: When the history cannot settle the source of orthostatic syncope, what is recommended?
opts: Empiric vasopressors in the clinic
Vasopressors such as norepinephrine and vasopressin are for the emergency department and intensive care only, not empiric clinic use.
Reassurance with no further work-up
An unexplained source needs confirmation. Reassurance alone leaves the real diagnosis, which is what treatment targets, unidentified.
Repeat tilt-table tests until positive
The tilt-table test belongs to the tachycardia syndrome and has low sensitivity. Repetition does not replace specialty confirmation.
Referral to the right specialty to confirm
Correct. History is the most important tool for the diagnosis, or for referring to the right specialty for confirmation when the source is still unclear.

set2.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
set2.q: Which feature characterizes chronic hypotension?
opts: It ends once the trigger is removed
Removal of a trigger fits acute and reflex hypotension. In chronic hypotension the cause may be unavoidable, so it persists.
Its underlying cause may be unavoidable
Correct. Chronic hypotension waxes and wanes, is intermittently symptomatic, and its underlying cause, such as a cardiomyopathy, may not be removable.
It always has one specific trigger
A specific trigger is typical of acute hypotension. Chronic hypotension is intermittent and may have a cause that cannot be avoided.
It is sudden and always symptomatic
Sudden onset with symptoms describes acute hypotension. Chronic hypotension is only intermittently symptomatic.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: Which symptoms occur on standing in postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome?
opts: Numb feet and dry mouth
Reduced sensation in the feet suggests diabetic neuropathy behind neurogenic orthostatic hypotension; a dry mouth suggests volume depletion.
Warmth and nausea while voiding
Warmth and nausea while voiding at night are the prodrome of situational micturition syncope, a reflex type.
Palpitations and lightheadedness
Correct. Tachycardia with or without lightheadedness, dizziness, fainting and palpitations appears on standing and usually eases when lying down.
Tongue biting and confusion
Tongue biting and prolonged confusion afterward point toward seizure, a separate non-hypotensive cause of loss of consciousness.

set2.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set2.q: Which cause of syncope is non-hypotensive?
opts: Volume depletion
Volume depletion lowers pressure on standing and is the typical cause of non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
Vasovagal reflex
The vasovagal reflex lowers pressure through bradycardia and vasodilation, making it a hypotensive cause of syncope.
Autonomic failure
Autonomic failure produces neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, a hypotensive cause with a minimal heart rate rise.
Hypoglycemia
Correct. Hypoglycemia is listed with seizure, toxic overdose, electrolyte imbalance, hypoxia, anxiety, anemia and the tachycardia syndrome as non-hypotensive causes.

set2.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set2.q: Which best describes a sign?
opts: The named disease that explains it
Identifying the disease, disorder or injury that explains the signs and symptoms is the diagnosis, not a sign.
A list of possible explanations
A list of conditions that could explain the findings is a differential diagnosis, which is built from signs and symptoms.
Objective, measurable evidence
Correct. A sign is objective and measurable, such as a standing blood pressure; a symptom is a subjective change that the patient feels and reports.
A change the patient reports
A subjective change that the patient feels and reports is a symptom, such as dizziness or lightheadedness.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: Which comorbidity is a reason to avoid midodrine?
opts: Recent diarrheal illness
Diarrhea causes volume depletion, which is managed by treating the underlying cause; it is not a listed midodrine contraindication.
Chronic kidney disease
Correct. Chronic kidney disease joins supine hypertension and severe heart disease as the settings in which midodrine is avoided.
Long-standing diabetes
Long-standing diabetes can cause neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, the condition midodrine is best suited to.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is associated with the tachycardia syndrome; it is not a listed reason to avoid midodrine.

set2.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set2.q: Which history points toward cardiogenic rather than reflex syncope?
opts: Fainting at the sight of blood
Fear and emotional stress are vasovagal triggers, so a faint at the sight of blood points to reflex syncope.
Fainting after urinating at night
Fainting during nocturnal voiding is situational micturition syncope, a reflex type rather than a cardiac cause.
Abrupt collapse without any warning
Correct. Abrupt syncope with minimal prodrome, often after brief palpitations, in someone with coronary disease or reduced ejection fraction points to a cardiac cause.
Warmth, nausea and sweating beforehand
A prodrome of warmth, nausea, sweating and lightheadedness followed by rapid recovery favors reflex syncope.

set2.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set2.q: Which condition can progress to syncope if the pressure keeps falling?
opts: Near-syncope
Correct. Near-syncope is the dizziness, lightheadedness and tunnel vision that precede syncope, so it is the warning phase before consciousness is lost.
Postictal state
A postictal state follows a seizure, and prolonged confusion afterward is a feature that points away from syncope rather than toward it.
Supine hypertension
Supine hypertension is high pressure while lying flat. It changes the orthostatic threshold to a fall of more than 30 mmHg rather than preceding a faint.
Relative bradycardia
A slow rate is one part of the vasovagal reflex chain. Near-syncope is the named symptom state that precedes the loss of consciousness itself.

set2.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set2.q: Which referral applies to all three types of cardiogenic syncope?
opts: Cardiology consultation
Correct. Arrhythmic, structural and vascular cardiogenic syncope each list cardiology consultation alongside their own tests.
Neurology consultation
Neurologic input suits autonomic failure or a suspected seizure; each cardiogenic type lists cardiology consultation instead.
Endocrinology referral
Endocrine disease such as diabetes causes neurogenic orthostatic hypotension; cardiogenic syncope is referred to cardiology.
Physical therapy referral
Physical therapy has no listed role in cardiogenic syncope, whose work-up pairs cardiac testing with cardiology consultation.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: What is known about the cause of vasovagal syncope?
opts: Structural heart disease
Structural heart disease, such as infarction, cardiomyopathy, heart failure or valve disease, causes cardiogenic syncope.
Unclear; possibly genetic
Correct. The etiology of vasovagal syncope is unclear, with a possible genetic predisposition, even though its triggers and reflex chain are well described.
Autonomic nerve damage
Autonomic nerve damage is the cause of neurogenic orthostatic syncope, in which the heart rate rises only minimally on standing.
Chronic volume depletion
Volume depletion causes non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, where the intact autonomic system raises the heart rate significantly.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: With a sensitivity near 40% and specificity above 80%, what does a negative tilt-table test mean?
opts: It reliably rules the syndrome out
Ruling out needs high sensitivity. At about 40%, most of the weight sits with a positive result instead.
It confirms autonomic failure
Autonomic failure is shown by a pressure fall with a minimal heart rate rise on orthostatic vitals, not by a negative tilt test.
It points to a cardiac cause
A negative tilt test says nothing about the heart. Cardiac causes are pursued with an electrocardiogram, monitoring or echocardiography.
It does little to exclude the syndrome
Correct. Low sensitivity means many patients with the syndrome test negative, so a negative result tells almost nothing, while a positive result carries more weight.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: Why is patient education central to hypotension management?
opts: It replaces the need to find a cause
Education supports treatment of the cause rather than replacing it; the real diagnosis still has to be found and treated.
It allows vasopressors to be stopped
Vasopressors belong in the emergency department and intensive care; education matters for the outpatient measures patients carry out themselves.
It shortens the orthostatic test
Education does not change the diagnostic criteria, which still require readings within 3 minutes of standing.
Understanding is the key to compliance
Correct. A patient who understands why the hypotension happens is far more likely to follow slow position changes, trigger avoidance and medication changes.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: Which chain of events produces vasovagal syncope?
opts: Sympathetic surge, tachycardia, constriction
A sympathetic surge would raise pressure. The vasovagal reflex runs the opposite way, with vagal dominance and sympathetic withdrawal.
Autonomic failure, fixed heart rate
A fall with a nearly fixed heart rate reflects autonomic failure, the neurogenic orthostatic pattern, rather than a transient reflex.
Fluid loss, compensatory tachycardia
Fluid loss with a compensatory heart rate rise is non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, showing an intact autonomic reflex.
Vagal surge, bradycardia, vasodilation
Correct. A transient rise in parasympathetic outflow with sympathetic inhibition causes bradycardia, vasodilation and reduced cardiac output, so systolic pressure falls.

set2.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
set2.q: What does symptomatic hypotension lead to?
opts: Seizure from cortical irritation
Seizure is listed among non-hypotensive causes of transient loss of consciousness. Symptomatic hypotension works through reduced brain perfusion instead.
Hypoglycemia from poor intake
Hypoglycemia is a separate, non-hypotensive cause of syncope. It is excluded with a blood glucose rather than being a product of low pressure.
Supine hypertension overnight
Supine hypertension is high pressure while lying flat, a comorbidity that changes the orthostatic threshold, not a consequence of symptomatic hypotension.
Syncope from cerebral hypoperfusion
Correct. Syncope is the result of symptomatic hypotension: low peripheral resistance or low cardiac output lowers pressure until brain perfusion falls and consciousness is briefly lost.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: Which drug is preferred when supine hypertension limits therapy?
opts: Phenylephrine
Phenylephrine is a pressor used only in the emergency department and intensive care, not an outpatient choice.
Norepinephrine
Norepinephrine is among the pressors reserved for the emergency department and intensive care.
Droxidopa
Correct. Droxidopa has mild efficacy but is better with supine hypertension (high pressure while lying flat), the setting in which midodrine is avoided.
Midodrine
Midodrine is avoided with supine hypertension, severe heart disease and chronic kidney disease, even though it is best with neurogenic syncope.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: What does a significant heart rate rise during an orthostatic pressure fall indicate?
opts: A primary cardiac arrhythmia
An arrhythmia is suspected from abrupt collapse with palpitations and is confirmed on an electrocardiogram, not by a reflex rise on standing.
A reflex surge in vagal tone
A vagal surge slows the heart rather than speeding it. That bradycardic chain describes vasovagal reflex syncope.
An intact sympathetic reflex response
Correct. A rise such as 68 to 92 per minute as pressure falls demonstrates an intact baroreceptor-mediated sympathetic response, which favors non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
Autonomic failure from diabetes
Autonomic failure blunts the heart rate response, so a diabetic autonomic neuropathy shows a minimal rather than a significant rise.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for hypotension in the lecture topic list for the following populations. a. infant b. child c. adolescent d. adult e. elderly
set2.q: Why must a blood pressure reading be interpreted against the patient's age?
opts: Age changes cuff accuracy only
The issue is the normal range, which shifts with age, not the accuracy of the measuring device.
Normal values change with age
Correct. Blood pressure norms are affected by age, so a reading that is normal for an adult may be abnormal for an infant or child, and the reverse.
Only adults can become hypotensive
Hypotension can occur at any age; the point is that the normal range itself differs between infants, children and adults.
Children tolerate any low pressure
Children have their own normal ranges, and a pressure below them is still hypotension. Age changes the reference, not the risk.

set2.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
set2.q: How is hypotension from infection classified by its time course?
opts: Brief and self-limited
Brief, self-limited episodes fit reflex syncope. Infection produces hypotension that lasts, even though it is acute in onset.
Intermittent and reflex
Intermittent reflex episodes are situational or vasovagal syncope, triggered by bodily functions or emotion rather than infection.
Long-lasting acute
Correct. Infection, including bacteremia, sepsis and septic shock, causes long-lasting acute hypotension, distinct from brief toxic causes and chronic cardiogenic ones.
Chronic and unavoidable
Chronic hypotension with a possibly unavoidable cause comes from cardiogenic disease such as reduced ejection fraction heart failure.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: In neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, how is volume status usually described?
opts: Volume status cannot be assessed
Volume status is assessed at the bedside, for example by mucous membranes, and it is one of the features used to separate the two forms.
Volume depletion is usually absent
Correct. The problem is autonomic failure rather than fluid, so mucous membranes are typically moist and there is no evidence of dehydration.
Volume depletion is often present
Volume depletion is often present in the non-neurogenic form, driven by diarrhea, hemorrhage or diuretics, which is its typical cause.
Volume overload is always present
Overload is not part of the comparison. Neurogenic patients usually have normal volume, with the fault in the autonomic response.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
set2.q: In which setting should midodrine be avoided?
opts: Supine hypertension
Correct. Midodrine is avoided with supine hypertension (high pressure while lying flat), severe heart disease and chronic kidney disease, despite being best with neurogenic syncope.
Diabetic neuropathy
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy causes neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, exactly the setting in which midodrine is best.
Parkinson disease
Parkinson disease is an example cause of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, where midodrine is the best listed drug.
Multiple system atrophy
Multiple system atrophy is a neurogenic cause, and neurogenic syncope is where midodrine is best used.

set2.io: Define hypotension
set2.q: How is hypotension defined?
opts: A systolic pressure under one fixed cutoff
No single cutoff applies to everyone. Norms are affected by age, and a reading must be judged against comorbidities and the possibility of relative hypotension.
Any faint that occurs on standing up
A faint on standing is syncope, a possible result of symptomatic hypotension, rather than the definition of hypotension itself.
A pressure drop only when symptoms occur
Symptoms are not part of the definition. Hypotension is the pressure falling below normal; symptomatic hypotension is what produces syncope.
A fall in systemic pressure below normal
Correct. Hypotension is a decrease in systemic blood pressure below the normal level, and what counts as normal shifts with age and with the patient's own baseline and comorbidities.
